## Summary
Alps Alpine is a Japanese component maker founded 1 November 1948 as Kataoka Electric, headquartered in Ota, Tokyo; Alps Electric and Alpine Electronics integrated as Alps Alpine on 1 January 2019 [1][3]. Its segments are Component, Sensor & Communication and Mobility; the company describes the second in terms of sensing, control and communications technology without naming a wireless standard [3][4]. All 43 MA-L blocks under this name (64:05:E4, BC:42:8C, 74:95:EC, 00:06:F7, 00:07:04, 00:06:F5, 34:C7:31, 64:D4:BD, 04:98:F3, 00:21:4F, 84:70:51, EC:D9:09 and C0:40:8D among them) are registered to plants in Miyagi and Fukushima - Kakuda, Furukawa (Osaki) and Soma - not to Tokyo [11]; the Japanese Wikipedia article lists the Kakuda and Furukawa plants among the company's sites [2]. Documented module silicon is Marvell 88W8887 in the UGKZ7A10 (802.11abgn+ac 1x1 with Bluetooth, SDIO) [7] and CSR8311 in the Bluetooth-only UGXZE-104A [8]; older UGJZ-series modules appear in a Broadcom reference card and Contec access points [10], and an ALPS UGFZC-001 sits in a Sony TV remote pad [9]. So a MAC in these blocks is most likely an Alps wireless module inside another maker's product [7][8][9][10]; given Alpine's OEM head-unit business with Honda, Volkswagen, Jaguar, Land Rover, BMW, Mercedes-Benz and the Chrysler brands [6], a vehicle is a plausible host, but no source reached names an automaker as a customer for the communication modules themselves, so that step is an inference. Alps also made keyboards for Apple, which carry no radio [1][5]. Note for lookups: a DeviWiki search for "Alps" also returns TP-Link, Netgear and Mercusys router pages carrying an ALPS tag [10]; those pages do not document an Alps Alpine module, so a search hit is not a hardware match. No FCC grantee code was found in the sources reached (FCC databases refused automated access), and MAC randomization behaviour is not documented.
